metadata.title: Claude, Amendment History.
metadata.purpose: Answer what actually governs a contract that's been amended more than once: the original document, or something else. Lands the carry-out that the contract in force today is the original with each clause replaced by its most recent edit -- check clause by clause, not document by document.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Someone reads the original contract, sees a signature, and assumes that document is the law. It isn't. Every amendment written since has edited that document, and the version in force today is a stitched-together thing. Real question: what does the contract say now?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What does the original contract say?', hesitates on 'original', corrects to 'current', lands the real question

props.text:

the original
contract say?

beats.narration_text: A contract gets signed, then amended twice over two years — a notice period changed once, a renewal date changed again. Ask what the contract says today and the reflex is to pull up the original signed document. Wrong artifact. The original only ever says what it said on day one; it has no mechanism for knowing anything came after. It's a snapshot, not a live document.

shot.new_visual_element: An original-contract card stamped 'DAY ONE'; two amendment chips slide past it, dim and disconnected, never touching it

production_viz.label: The original only knows day one
production_viz.mechanic: A card labelled 'ORIGINAL CONTRACT' with a 'DAY ONE' stamp, fully lit. Two dim, unlit chips labelled 'amendment 1' and 'amendment 2' slide in from the side and pass underneath the original card without touching it. A caption fades in beneath: 'it can't know what came after.'

beats.narration_text: Amendment history walks the chain in order. For any one clause, only the last edit counts — not the sum, not the average, just the most recent one. Watch a single clause: a lease's notice period. Original contract set it at thirty days. First amendment stretched it to sixty. Second amendment cut it back to forty-five. Three edits, one field, last one wins.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three cards in a row overwriting the same NOTICE field: 30 -> 60 -> 45

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- only the last edit counts
production_viz.mechanic: Three cards left to right: 'ORIGINAL' showing 'NOTICE: 30 DAYS', 'AMENDMENT 1' showing 'NOTICE: 60 DAYS', 'AMENDMENT 2' showing 'NOTICE: 45 DAYS'. Each card in turn dims the one before it as it lands. THIS EXACT THREE-CARD CHAIN RETURNS, RESOLVED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: So today, notice is forty-five days — not thirty, not sixty. Whichever edit landed last, and only for that one clause. Here's the trade-off the design makes: a clause no amendment ever touched isn't missing from the picture — the original wording still governs it. And an amendment sitting somewhere in the file doesn't mean it touched the clause you're asking about. You track each clause's own chain, one clause at a time, not the contract's.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the 45 card locks in and highlights; then splits into 'untouched clause -> original still governs' and 'amendment exists != this clause changed'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- last edit wins, and only for that clause
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 THREE-CARD CHAIN RETURNS, identical placement, and collapses into one card reading 'NOTICE: 45 DAYS', highlighted terracotta -- '30' and '60' visibly crossed and dimmed beside it. It then splits into two cards: left reads 'payment clause: no amendment ever touched it' with a steady, unedited card labelled 'original still governs'; right reads 'amendment 2 exists' beside a separate, unrelated clause card connected only by a dashed line labelled 'check its own chain'.

beats.narration_text: The contract in force today isn't the original, and it isn't the amendments -- it's the original with each clause replaced by its most recent edit. Check clause by clause, not document by document.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Attach a contract and every amendment to it, then say: walk through this clause by clause. For each one, tell me whether an amendment changed it, and if so, give me only the most recent version — not the original. Go deeper: ask which clauses stayed untouched, and which fields got edited more than once. Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm reviewing a contract that has been amended more than once, and I need to know what it actually says today, clause by clause. I'll paste in the original contract and every amendment to it, in order. Walk through the contract clause by clause. For each clause, tell me whether any amendment changed it, and if so, give me only the most recent version of that clause — not the original, not intermediate edits. If no amendment ever touched a clause, say so and quote the original wording. Return the result as a table: clause name, current wording, source (original / amendment 1 / amendment 2 / …).
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: ask which clauses stayed untouched across every amendment, and which fields got edited more than once — those are the ones where the chain, not just the last edit, tells the real story.
